synopsis: The booklet recommends layered braking models per machine family: a calibrated point-mass core with measured latency, brake build-up lag and conservative deceleration by grade, payload and surface, supplemented by stability challenges and selected high-fidelity edge cases rather than one ultimate digital twin [f146, f13840]. Higher fidelity is justified for brake hydraulics and latency spread, articulated or high-center-of-gravity stability, state-dependent hydrostatic braking, and soft or deformable ground [f5906]. The runtime trigger should remain small, identifiable and conservative, while richer offline models challenge its safety assumptions; the selection rule is the lowest fidelity that predicts every safety-relevant output within a validated uncertainty envelope [f6074, f6075, f13837]. Complexity is not an accuracy guarantee: in a 2026 on-road round robin, point-mass implementations reproduced the prescribed profile exactly, while more complex models produced spreads of 0.033 s and 0.314 m [f5907, f5908]. No universal off-road prediction error is supplied for any fidelity level, and evidence of heavy-machine braking-distance fidelity on loose and wet surfaces was not found, so each level must be checked against the program’s own physical tests [f13842, f4307, f13843]. Detailed terrain simulations are too costly for exhaustive sweeps and can be dominated by uncertain soil inputs; the proposed alternative is to learn soil effects with richer models, fit simpler models for regression testing, confirm their envelope physically, and avoid surrogate extrapolation outside the trained domain [f6103, f6104, f15994, f6106].
